title: Organised crime inside the state
summary:
Drug traffickers, mafias, smuggling rings and gangs get their own people inside the institutions meant to stop them, and this map records it in 90 countries, in cases from the 1950s to this year. Where a cartel's routes run through a port or a border town, it tends to buy the officials who stand in the way, such as customs inspectors, the local police commander and sometimes the judge, so that the shipment is waved through and the case never reaches court. What the groups want is much the same everywhere: no arrest, no extradition, warning before a raid and safe passage for their goods.

The record is thickest along the cocaine routes. From the Andes through Central America, the Caribbean and Mexico to the US border, traffickers have bought police chiefs, generals, governors and judges, and in parts of Mexico whole town police forces have worked for a cartel. Across the Atlantic, the same trade passes through small West African and Sahel states and into the container ports of Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany and Spain, where networks recruit dock workers, customs staff and police. In northern Europe and Israel the usual purchase is information: officers and clerks sell case files and police register data.

In other places the criminal holds office himself. Gang leaders and traffickers have sat in the parliaments and assemblies of India, Pakistan, Taiwan, Syria, the Dominican Republic and Brazil. In Cambodia and Myanmar the owners of compounds that run online scams have been protected by politicians, and some became senators, advisers to prime ministers or rulers of a border zone.

At the top of the state, Italy has dissolved town councils and health authorities 402 times since 1991 because a mafia group had taken hold of them, and in Colombia roughly 30% of Congress was investigated or convicted over collusion with paramilitary armies that also exported cocaine. A former president of Honduras, Juan Orlando Hernández, was convicted in New York of taking traffickers' bribes, and was later freed by a US pardon.

For people who live with this, reporting a trafficker can mean reporting to someone the trafficker pays, and a judge may have been paid before a case is heard. Victims and witnesses have no safe court to turn to. Much of this came out through trials abroad, and an official charged in another country can stay in office at home.
uncertain: Several cases rest on US indictments, sanctions or trial testimony that no court has tested against the person named. Some of the protection alleged for scam-compound owners in Cambodia and Myanmar comes from sanctions and press investigations rather than court findings.

title: China's long arm abroad
summary:
China's Communist Party runs a department, the United Front Work Department, whose job is to win friends and influence among Chinese communities, business people and politicians abroad. It works through friendship associations, hometown clubs and councils for 'peaceful reunification' with Taiwan. Alongside it, China's main spy agency, the Ministry of State Security, and military intelligence recruit people close to power. Courts, security services and parliamentary inquiries in more than a dozen countries, from the Pacific islands and Southeast Asia to North America and Europe, have found them reaching into parties, election campaigns, ministers' offices, parliaments, city halls and defence and research work.

Taiwan, which Beijing claims as its own, has more cases on this map than anywhere else. Mainland money pays for small parties' campaigns and for village chiefs' trips to the mainland, and Beijing recruits retired admirals, former cabinet officials and aides inside the governing party.

In Australia, New Zealand, Canada, Britain and the United States, the usual route is a well-connected donor or community leader who chairs a United Front-linked group, gives to parties and gets close to MPs; Canada's 2025 public inquiry found China to be the most active foreign state interfering in the country. The reach goes down to local government, and in 2026 the mayor of a Californian city pleaded guilty to acting as a Chinese agent. In Europe, the people working for Chinese intelligence or Party bodies have included a former senator, an MEP's aide and an adviser to a president, and in North America others have worked inside defence contractors and government laboratories, passing technology to China.

In the Pacific islands the money goes straight to lawmakers, and in the Solomon Islands a Chinese-funded account run by the prime minister's office paid 39 of the 50 MPs weeks before a vote on removing him. Inside UN agencies, Chinese nationals in senior posts have been accused of using them for Beijing; a former head of the UN's economic department said on Chinese television that he had a Uyghur leader removed from a UN forum.

For voters, this means some candidates on the ballot, from parliament down to the city council, were chosen, paid for or run on Beijing's instructions without voters being told, and some MPs vote after taking money that started in China. Many cases end without a conviction, because the money passes through middlemen and intelligence reports seldom name names.
uncertain: The former UN official's account of having a Uyghur leader removed from a UN forum is his own statement on Chinese television. Accusations that other Chinese nationals in senior UN posts served Beijing come from critics and governments, not from any finding by the UN. Several of the European and North American cases are charges or security-service findings that have not been tested in court.

title: Russia's networks in Europe and Africa
summary:
Russia reaches into other countries' politics by two routes, and which one it uses depends on how strong the state it is dealing with is. Where a government is weak and fighting rebels, as in parts of Central and West Africa, Russia places its own people beside the head of state. Where a government is strong and elected, as across the European Union and its neighbours, it works through individual politicians, paying them or running them as sources, so that a speech, a vote or a party's line serves Moscow while appearing to be the politician's own.

In Africa the main vehicle was the Wagner Group, a private military company run by the businessman Yevgeny Prigozhin. It placed advisers inside governments and, in Madagascar, Prigozhin's political strategists paid candidates in a presidential election. In the Central African Republic a Wagner-linked Russian became the president's national security adviser in 2018, so advice on who the state should fight came partly from Moscow.

In Europe the money tends to travel through go-betweens: a pro-Kremlin Ukrainian politician, a banker, a cultural association, a small news website. The clearest example is Voice of Europe, a site run from Prague that passed Russian money to politicians in several EU countries until Czech intelligence exposed it in 2024. Members of the European Parliament from Britain, Germany, Latvia and Hungary appear in these cases as having taken Russian money or reported to Russian intelligence. In some countries it reached the top of national parties: in Italy an associate of the League's leader negotiated secret oil money for the party, in Ukraine a close ally of Vladimir Putin led the main opposition party, and in Moldova Russia funded a whole party and a court jailed one of its elected governors for taking undeclared Russian money.

For people living in these countries, it means a politician they voted for may be speaking for a foreign government without their knowing. In the Central African Republic it means the president's security adviser answered partly to another state. Almost none of this was declared by the politicians involved; it came out through intelligence services, leaked emails and recordings, and trials.
uncertain: Several cases rest on sanctions, intelligence briefings, leaked emails or recordings, or press reporting rather than court rulings. The German and Latvian MEPs have not been convicted, the Italian oil deal is known from a leaked recording, and the Ukrainian opposition leader's treason charge rests on the Ukrainian government's case.

In the 1970s the Korean Central Intelligence Agency and businessman Tongsun Park paid US congressmen ('Koreagate'); the House Fraser subcommittee (1978) also examined the KCIA's use of Sun Myung Moon's organisations.

summary:
Governments reach into other countries by paying, or planting, people who hold office there: legislators, diplomats, ministers' aides, members of the European Parliament, UN officials and staff at technology companies. The cases run from the 1970s to today, and the sponsors range from neighbours to distant powers, among them Russia, China, India, Iran, Egypt, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Azerbaijan, Morocco, Hungary, Cuba, South Korea, and earlier Saddam Hussein's Iraq and Muammar Gaddafi's Libya. The money rarely goes straight from one government to an official. It passes through a businessman, a lobbyist or a company the foreign state controls, so that on paper it looks like a gift, a consulting fee, free travel or a campaign donation.

The targets are not only national governments. Saddam's Iraq gave oil allocations to the head of the UN's Oil-for-Food programme, North Korea chose the local staff of a UN agency and kept their pay, and Hungarian intelligence officers at Hungary's EU mission tried to recruit European Commission staff.

Most documented cases are in the United States, Canada and Brussels, largely because those places have prosecutors and oversight bodies that publish what they find; 13 of the 31 cases in this pattern are American. In 2024 a New York jury convicted Senator Bob Menendez, who chaired the committee that shapes US arms sales, of acting as Egypt's agent for cash and gold bars. Spy services go further and place their own people inside the state for decades; Cuba's intelligence service had an officer in the US diplomatic service for more than 40 years, rising to ambassador. At the far end, one government takes over another's offices outright: UN experts report that Rwanda's army commands the M23 armed group in eastern Congo and has put Rwandans in charge of mining, tax, banking and border control in the areas it holds.

For the people living there, the result is officials who answer to someone they did not elect. Votes in a parliament or an international body, an arms decision or a provincial tax office can be bought for another country's benefit. Many cases stop short of a verdict. Canada's parliamentary intelligence committee found that some MPs and senators knowingly took part in foreign interference but named none of them, and several US cases ended in acquittal, dismissal or a pardon, leaving voters without a settled account.
uncertain: Rwanda's command of M23 rests on UN expert reports, not a court verdict, and Rwanda denies it. India rejects the Canadian findings. The Oil-for-Food payment to the programme's head is the finding of an independent inquiry, not a conviction.

title: Foreign money inside Europe's parliaments
summary:
Governments that want a softer report on their human-rights record, a vote on trade or a friendly speech pay members of Europe's parliaments to deliver it. The targets are the European Parliament in Brussels, the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, where MPs from 46 countries judge elections and human rights, and national parliaments whose members also sit in those bodies. The payers in the cases on this map are Azerbaijan, Qatar, Morocco and Russia, along with Chinese state interests and the Chinese telecoms company Huawei, and the same methods have now reached the circle around Israel's prime minister.

The money rarely arrives as a plain bribe. It comes as consultancy fees routed through shell companies, as cash passed through a human-rights charity, as paid advertising in an MP's newspaper, as gifts, travel and football tickets, or as payments from a go-between in a third country, sometimes a former MP. Russia's money has come through a pro-Kremlin Ukrainian politician and a Prague news site he ran. Alongside the money, Russian and Chinese intelligence have placed or recruited people inside the European Parliament, from MEPs to assistants. Leaked bank records, police raids and seized cash are how most of it has come out.

Azerbaijan's network is the widest. The so-called Azerbaijani Laundromat moved $2.9 billion through shell companies, some of it to European politicians, and an inquiry found in 2018 that Azerbaijani money had reached Assembly members from at least six countries; one of them, an Italian group leader later jailed for it, helped defeat a report on the people Azerbaijan jails for their politics. In 2022 Belgian police found bags of cash at the home of a European Parliament vice-president in a case prosecutors say was paid for by Qatar and Morocco. Courts in Italy, Germany, Hungary and Britain have now convicted current or former members.

For voters, this means the person they elected may be speaking and voting for another government on human rights, trade or security, and they cannot see it until police find the money. The people most directly harmed are those the reports were meant to protect: prisoners, opposition figures and journalists in the paying countries. Cases take years, and accused members keep their seats while parliament decides whether to lift the immunity that protects them from prosecution.
uncertain: The Qatar and Morocco case in Brussels, the Huawei case and the Israeli case are investigations or charges, not convictions; Belgian prosecutors later said one MEP named in the Huawei case was a different man with the same name.

title: Turkey's long arm: chasing the Gülen movement
roles: Country that handed people over or closed schools
summary:
Since the failed military coup of July 2016, Turkey's government has treated the Gülen movement, a religious network led by the preacher Fethullah Gülen that ran schools and businesses in many countries, as an enemy that had hidden itself inside the state. It says Gülen followers spent decades taking posts in the police, courts and army, calls the movement a terrorist group, 'FETÖ', and blames it for the coup. The movement denies organising the coup, though Turkish courts have convicted hundreds of officers for it.

Part of how followers got in is on the record. The questions for Turkey's 2010 civil-service entrance exam were leaked in advance, which helped place Gülen followers in state jobs, and in the same year candidates linked to the movement won control of the board that appoints and promotes judges and prosecutors. Prosecutors and gendarmes tied to the movement later turned those posts against the government, summoning the head of the national intelligence agency for questioning and stopping its lorries.

Inside Turkey, the response has been removal by decree rather than by trial. About 150,000 people lost public jobs after the coup without a court ruling on each person, among them judges, police officers, soldiers and teachers. The clearest single instance came the day after the coup, when about a third of Turkey's judges were removed at once. The label has since reached a deputy head of the Constitutional Court and a judge at a UN war-crimes tribunal.

The Gülen movement is not the first group to get inside the Turkish state. In the 1970s the leader of the Grey Wolves, the militant youth wing of a nationalist party, served as deputy prime minister, and in 1996 a car crash at Susurluk showed a wanted Grey Wolves gunman travelling with a senior police officer and a member of parliament. Abroad, the Gülen movement has reached into foreign politics in its own right: in the United States, groups tied to it paid for about 200 trips to Turkey for members of Congress and their staff.

For Turks, it has meant a justice system where a prosecutor's or judge's first loyalty could lie with a movement, followed by one where being named as a Gülen follower can cost a teacher, judge or police officer their job with no individual hearing.
uncertain: Turkish courts accepted that the Gülen movement organised the 2016 coup, but the movement denies it. The movement's role in the 2010 judicial board election rests largely on later Turkish government and court accounts, and the convictions of the Constitutional Court deputy head and the UN tribunal judge are disputed.

title: Churches and movements placing members in the state
summary:
Religious movements and church-linked lobbies get their members into ministries, parliaments, courts and police forces in about 30 countries on this map, from Japan and South Korea through India, Indonesia, Turkey and Senegal to Brazil, Spain and the United States. Most do it openly. A movement trains politicians or builds a parliamentary league or party of its own, and its members vote together on schools, family law, abortion and the constitution. Others supply what campaigns need: volunteers, donations, a congregation's votes, or mass sign-ups to a party so their members weigh heavily when candidates are chosen.

In some countries one movement shapes most of the government. In India the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), a Hindu nationalist volunteer organisation, trains many of the people who run the governing BJP; a press count found that 38 of the 53 BJP ministers in Narendra Modi's second government had RSS roots. In Japan, 10 of the 19 ministers in the cabinet formed in 2025 belong to the parliamentary league of Nippon Kaigi, a nationalist lobby. Evangelical churches hold a voting bloc of more than 200 of the 513 seats in Brazil's lower house, and Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation that encourages lay members to carry their faith into public life, has had members in ministries across Spain and Latin America since the 1950s.

Money is the main tool of the movements with the widest reach. The Unification Church, a Korean-founded movement, has given cash, gifts and campaign help to politicians in Japan, South Korea and the United States; in 2022 Japan's governing party found that 179 of its 379 members of parliament had ties to it, and in 2026 South Korean courts jailed the church's leader for bribing politicians.

A few movements have placed members in secret. In the 1970s the Church of Scientology planted a member as a clerk inside the US tax authority to copy its files. Turkey says the Gülen movement, a religious network, spent decades placing followers as police, judges and officers; after the failed 2016 coup the government dismissed about 150,000 public employees by decree, without a court ruling on each person.

Where many ministers share one movement's training, people outside it find laws on religion, schooling and the constitution written without them. Where a church buys access, its members' donations become political money and party primaries can be decided by congregations signed up in bulk.
uncertain: Membership of a lawful religious group or lobby is not wrongdoing, and several membership counts, including the RSS and Nippon Kaigi figures, come from press reports and league lists, not official records. Turkey's account of Gülen placements rests largely on government decrees, not individual court findings.

title: Religious nationalism in power
summary:
In parts of South and East Asia, movements that want the state to defend one religion, or one national identity tied to a religion, have their members in cabinet, in parliament, on law-drafting panels and on public boards. Most of it is lawful and visible in membership lists and appointments.

In India and Japan the route is through the governing party. In India, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), a Hindu nationalist volunteer organisation, is the body from which the governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) grew. It lends the party organisers and supplies much of its leadership: Prime Minister Narendra Modi was a full-time RSS organiser, and a 2020 count by the news site ThePrint found that 38 of the 53 BJP ministers had RSS roots. Its people have also been placed on the central bank's board and at the head of the national history research council, and an investigation found that 62% of India's new military feeder schools went to RSS-linked bodies and BJP figures. In Japan, a nationalist lobby, Nippon Kaigi, and the political arm of the Shinto shrine association each keep a league of members of parliament that backs constitutional revision and official honours for the Yasukuni Shrine, where Japan's war dead, including convicted war criminals, are enshrined. Press counts put 15 of the 19 ministers in Shinzo Abe's 2014 cabinet in Nippon Kaigi's league, and 10 of 19 in the cabinet Sanae Takaichi, herself a league member, formed in 2025.

In Buddhist-majority Myanmar and Sri Lanka, monks' movements have been given a direct hand in writing the law. In Myanmar, texts proposed by Ma Ba Tha, a Buddhist nationalist monks' group, became four laws in 2015 that regulate religious conversion and marriage between Buddhist women and men of other faiths. In Sri Lanka, a president put the leader of an anti-Muslim monks' group in charge of drafting a single legal code.

In Bangladesh and Pakistan the route is covert. Hizb ut-Tahrir, a movement that campaigns for one Islamic state across Muslim countries, has recruited serving army officers, including a Pakistani brigadier, and in Bangladesh officers linked to it were accused of plotting a coup in 2012.

For religious minorities, this means living under laws and officials shaped by groups that favour the majority faith, in matters as close to home as whom they may marry, whether they may change religion and who runs their children's schools.
uncertain: The Japanese counts come from a Communist Party newspaper and press reports of league lists, not from official records. The RSS does not publish membership rolls, so counts of ministers with RSS roots are journalists' estimates, and the figure for military schools comes from investigative reporting, not an official review.

title: Consultants and lobbyists inside the ministries
summary:
Governments hire consulting, accounting and lobbying firms to redesign agencies and draft laws, and the same firms sell advice to the companies those laws cover. Most of this is lawful. The cases here are where the arrangement let a firm, or the company paying it, steer the state from inside. They come mostly from Britain, the Commonwealth and the EU, where these firms do the most government work, with others in Africa where Western firms dealt with state companies.

The commonest route is people moving between the firm and the ministry. Partners and staff are lent to a treasury or a cabinet office to help write rules, then return to advise clients on the same rules; in Australia a PwC partner advising the Treasury on tax-avoidance law shared its confidential plans with dozens of PwC colleagues. A second route is former ministers and commissioners lobbying their old colleagues, or a financier given a desk at the centre of government, as Greensill Capital's founder was in Downing Street. A third is a company getting a minister or head of government to argue its case inside the cabinet, as happened for Uber in France and for the engineering firm SNC-Lavalin in Canada.

At the far end, a consultancy can help capture a whole institution. In South Africa a judicial inquiry found that Bain & Company, a US consultancy, helped President Jacob Zuma's allies take control of the national tax service, and its restructuring cut the unit that produced a third of the service's revenue. In the same years foreign consultancies paid officials at South Africa's state power and rail companies to win contracts, and Canadian engineers paid officials in Gaddafi-era Libya.

For taxpayers, it means a law can be shaped by advisers whose paying clients gain from its gaps, and the shortfall falls on everyone else. Because consulting reports are usually unpublished, voters cannot see who shaped a policy. In South Africa it meant a weaker tax service at the moment it was investigating corruption. Most of this came out through public inquiries, leaked files and court cases, not through routine disclosure.
uncertain: Bain denies that it knowingly helped take over South Africa's tax service. The French Uber case rests on leaked company files (the 'Uber Files').

title: Global firms buying governments
summary:
Large companies win public contracts and favourable laws by paying the officials who decide them, and this map records it in 27 countries. The pattern is strongest wherever the state owns the valuable asset: oil and mining across West, Central and southern Africa and Latin America, state investment funds, road and port contracts and power utilities. The payers are construction groups, commodity traders, shipbuilders, banks and utilities, and the money moves through intermediaries, shell companies or a department set up for the purpose, so the bribe appears as a consulting fee or a campaign donation.

The largest case is Odebrecht, a Brazilian construction group that admitted to US authorities in 2016 that it paid $788 million in bribes across Latin America and Africa; its money reached presidents, vice-presidents and campaigns from Mexico, Panama and the Dominican Republic to Peru, Ecuador and Angola. Swiss-based commodity traders, firms that buy and sell oil and metals, have admitted bribing officials at state oil companies in Nigeria, Congo, Angola, Brazil, Ecuador and several other countries. State borrowing is another route: in Malaysia and Mozambique, bankers and a shipbuilder paid officials while arranging loans and bonds that left the public with the debt.

In a few places a business reached the cabinet itself. In South Africa a judicial inquiry found that ministers and heads of state companies acted corruptly for the Gupta family, businessmen close to President Jacob Zuma who offered ministries to officials willing to cooperate. The same pattern appears in rich democracies on a smaller scale, where power companies in the United States have paid state lawmakers to pass laws in their favour.

Alongside the bribes runs a legal route. Senior staff of the investment bank Goldman Sachs have moved into the top economic posts of the United States, Italy, Germany, Canada, Portugal and Greece, into the New York Federal Reserve that supervises the bank, and into the World Bank, where they set rules that apply to their former employer.

Most of what is known came out through US and Swiss prosecutions, because those countries can charge foreign companies that use their banks. The cost falls on the public. Bribes are added to the price of roads, power and oil deals, countries lose revenue on resources sold cheaply, and in Peru and Ecuador the courts found that the leaders who awarded the contracts were the ones who were paid.
uncertain: No court has found the moves of Goldman Sachs staff into government illegal.

title: Industries inside their regulators
summary:
Companies get inside the bodies that are meant to regulate them, buy from them or write the rules for their industry. They do it in three ways: paying officials, putting their own people in official posts, and handing regulators and lawmakers text that is adopted as the official version. The record on this map covers more than 30 countries on every inhabited continent.

Paying officials is the best documented, because companies often settle with US, British or Swiss prosecutors afterwards. Consultancies, builders, commodity traders, arms makers and tobacco companies from the United States, Europe and Brazil have paid, or been charged with paying, officials at state power companies, oil companies, tax services and ministries across Africa, Latin America and Asia, to win contracts or, for tobacco firms, to block health laws. The largest single case is the Brazilian builder Odebrecht, which admitted paying $788 million in bribes in a dozen countries to win public works. In Britain and the United States, legislators have been paid to table questions or pass laws for the payer.

The second route is the revolving door, most visible in Washington, where in the late 2010s the environment, interior, defence and health departments and the telecoms regulator were each run by a former lawyer, lobbyist or executive from an industry the post oversees.

The third is getting inside the rule-making itself. Regulators of nuclear power, aircraft, medicines, food and pesticides in the United States, Japan, China and Europe have let the industries they oversee check their own products, draft passages of official reviews or keep an office inside the agency. Japan's parliamentary inquiry into the Fukushima meltdown found that the nuclear regulator had been captured by the power company it oversaw. In US state legislatures, thousands of bills have been copied almost word for word from industry-funded models. Oil, shipping and tobacco interests have worked inside UN bodies that set rules for their trades, and the hosts of two recent UN climate summits put executives from their state oil companies in charge.

For the public, the cost shows up in safety, prices and tax money. In the United States, Boeing employees still carry out much of the safety certification of Boeing planes, a system a congressional committee found weakened oversight before two crashes killed 346 people. Contracts won by bribery are paid from public budgets, and people live under rules written to suit the companies.
uncertain: Some cases rest on reporting, not on findings. The US appointments from industry were lawful and made in public; what they show is where officials came from, not that any decision was bought.

title: Scam compounds and casino money inside Asian states
summary:
In parts of South-East Asia, companies that run online scams and gambling aimed at people in China and around the world have got their owners into local office or into the circle around national leaders. The scams are run from guarded compounds where trafficked workers are held and forced to defraud strangers online, and the political ties are what let the compounds operate in the open.

The pattern is clearest in Cambodia and the Philippines. In Cambodia, business figures tied to the compounds have held honorary titles, advisory posts and a seat in the Senate, and relatives of the ruling family have owned stakes in the payment firms the money passes through. In the Philippines, the state licensed Chinese-run offshore gambling firms from 2016, and some of them used local office-holders to set up and protect large compounds in provincial towns.

Three cases show the shape of it. Chen Zhi, who built the Prince Group into one of Cambodia's largest conglomerates and served as an official adviser to Hun Sen and other leaders, was indicted by the United States in 2025 as the head of a cyber-fraud business, and Cambodia later sent him to China. Huione Group, a Phnom Penh financial firm whose payment arm counted a cousin of Prime Minister Hun Manet among its owners and directors, was named by the US Treasury as having laundered over $4 billion. In the Philippines, Alice Guo, mayor of the town where a scam compound was raided, was found to be a Chinese citizen who could never lawfully hold office, and was jailed for life for human trafficking.

For the people trafficked into these compounds, and for their families, a mayor or a relative of the head of government standing near the business leaves few safe places to complain. For victims abroad, stolen savings can pass through payment firms owned by people close to power. The Philippines has since banned the industry and charged officials; in Cambodia most of the action so far has come from the United States, Britain and China rather than from Cambodian courts.
uncertain: The charges against Chen Zhi have not been tried. The US Treasury finding on Huione is an administrative decision by one government, not a court verdict.

title: Iran's armed allies inside governments
roles: Where they sit in the state
summary:
Iran's Revolutionary Guards, through their foreign branch the Quds Force, arm and fund Shia militias and parties across the Middle East, and in some countries those groups have moved inside the state. They are written into the armed forces by law, they hold seats in parliament and the cabinet, their commanders run interior ministries, or their business partners hold state monopolies. Iran gets fighters that another country's budget pays for, and a say in other governments' decisions. The cases on this map run from 2005 to today.

Iraq is the clearest case. Since 2005, commanders of the Badr Organization, a militia founded in Iran, have more than once run Iraq's Interior Ministry, which controls the police. Since a 2016 law, the Popular Mobilization Forces, a coalition of about 67 armed groups almost all backed by the Guards, have been a branch of Iraq's armed forces paid from the state budget, and in 2024 their chief of staff said publicly that they took orders from Iran's supreme leader. Some of the brigades on that payroll are staffed by groups the United States lists as terrorist organisations, and their leaders also sit in parliament. In Lebanon, Hezbollah, a Shia party with its own armed wing aligned with Iran, chooses ministers in each government while refusing to hand its weapons to the state; after its fighters took control of west Beirut in 2008 it won a veto over cabinet decisions.

The same network reaches further out through money. In West Africa and South America, the US Treasury says people tied to Hezbollah got close to presidents through business deals or bribes, including in Paraguay; in Gambia, under President Yahya Jammeh, they received the fuel supply monopoly and half the state telecoms companies.

For people in these countries, it means taxes pay for armed units that answer to another country's leader, police commanded by men whose militia was founded abroad, and a cabinet that cannot settle questions of war and peace by itself, because one party at the table keeps its own army. Where Hezbollah's backers held monopolies, ordinary people paid for fuel and phone calls through companies whose profits, by one journalists' estimate, sent more than $100 million on to Hezbollah. Outside the Middle East, much of the evidence is US sanctions, which are one government's finding, not a court verdict.
uncertain: The figure of more than $100 million reaching Hezbollah through these monopolies is one journalists' estimate. Much of the evidence outside the Middle East, including the claims about Paraguay's leaders, is US sanctions, not court verdicts.
case_role: Where they sit in the state

title: Private forums where officials meet money
summary:
Private clubs, societies, conferences and think tanks bring officials together with business leaders and like-minded allies, away from the public record. Belonging to them is lawful. What the record shows is how often their members go on to hold the offices that set policy: for more than 80 years in the United States, and in Britain, Western Europe, Latin America and Australia as well.

The methods differ. Foreign-policy clubs such as the Council on Foreign Relations and the Trilateral Commission gather future officials before they take office; a 1977 study found that more than half of the senior US officials it surveyed between 1945 and 1972 were members of the Council. Skull and Bones, a secret society at Yale University, has supplied war and treasury secretaries, a CIA director and president, and in 2004 both main candidates for president. Legal and policy networks build lists of people to appoint and programmes for them to carry out: 43 of the 51 appeals-court judges in President Trump's first term were members of the Federalist Society, a network of conservative lawyers, The Reagan administration acted on about 60% of the 2,000 proposals in the Heritage Foundation's 1981 plan for it, and authors of the foundation's Project 2025 now staff Trump's second term. Democratic administrations draw on think tanks too, and staff of the Center for American Progress filled posts in the Biden White House. Industry-funded groups such as ALEC write model bills that state legislators file as their own; a 2019 investigation found at least 10,000 such copied bills in US states, more than 2,100 of which became law.

Other forums work internationally. The World Economic Forum, which runs the Davos meetings, picks about 100 people under 40 each year for its Young Global Leaders programme, and its alumni include serving heads of government and ministers. The free-market think tanks of the Atlas Network have had members in cabinets and public posts from Britain and Australia to Chile and Argentina; in Venezuela in 2002 the director of one of them signed the decree of a short-lived coup government.

For voters, it means some decisions are talked through first with people they never elected, in private meetings, and some laws carry wording written by companies. A judge picked through one legal network can shape rulings for decades after the president who chose them has left office.

title: Movements that sought the state itself

countries.note: A military court convicted Brigadier Ali Khan and four majors in 2012 of links to Hizb ut-Tahrir.
The army said in January 2012 it had stopped a coup by serving and retired officers linked to Hizb ut-Tahrir.

summary:
Some movements aim to take over the state itself rather than steer it from outside. Across the Arab world the main example is the Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement founded in Egypt in 1928 that works to bring its members into power, together with the parties that grew out of it. A smaller movement, Hizb ut-Tahrir, wants a single Islamic state, or caliphate, and has tried to get there by recruiting army officers.

In most countries the Brotherhood tradition has gone through elections. Parties from it have won seats and cabinet posts in Egypt, Jordan, Kuwait, Libya and Morocco, and in several of these led the government or became the largest party in parliament. The usual sequence afterwards is that the army or the palace pushes back: the party is removed, its leaders jailed and the movement banned. The clearest case is Egypt, where the Brotherhood's Mohamed Morsi won the presidency in 2012, the army removed him a year later and the government declared the group a terrorist organisation.

Sudan shows the other route. In 1989 Omar al-Bashir took power in a coup organised with the National Islamic Front, a movement derived from the Brotherhood, and over 30 years its supporters were placed in state jobs, including the courts, building on posts the movement had held since its leader became attorney general in 1979. Its leaders and an allied militia still hold posts and fight beside the army in the current war, and several have been sanctioned by the United States and Europe. Hizb ut-Tahrir has tried the army more directly: in 2012 a Pakistani military court convicted a brigadier and four majors of links to it, and in the same year Bangladesh's army linked it to a coup plot by serving officers.

For voters in these countries, it has meant seeing parties they elected win office and then be banned, with membership now punishable by prison in Egypt. In Sudan, people placed by the old regime still hold posts, and Islamist militias have a say in whether civilian rule returns. Governments in the Gulf and in France also accuse the movement of working its way into schools, ministries and local politics, accusations that the groups named reject.
uncertain: Morocco's PJD says it has no organisational link to the Egyptian Brotherhood. The 2025 French government report's findings are rejected by Musulmans de France.

title: Lodges inside police forces and courts
summary:
Freemasonry is a fraternal society whose members meet in private lodges and promise to help one another, and joining a lawful lodge is not a crime. The problem arises when police officers, judges and military officers belong to a lodge without saying so. A person in court cannot then know whether the officer or judge handling the case shares a membership with the other side. The cases on this map come from Britain, Italy, Argentina, the United States, Romania and Gabon, and span nearly two centuries, from a Masonic sheriff convicted in New York in 1827 over the abduction of a former member to declarations made by London police in 2026.

In the United States the brotherhood in question has sometimes been the Ku Klux Klan, a white-supremacist secret society. In the 1920s a Klansman mayor of Denver made a fellow Klansman his police chief, a Supreme Court justice reached the bench without his past membership being known, and Klan members have been found serving in a small Florida police force in 2014.

In Britain the issue has been how widespread membership is in police forces and courts and whether it should be declared. Parliamentary committees in the 1990s found the governing Grand Lodge slow to say which members served as police or judges. Earlier complaints include claims that lodge loyalties obstructed police corruption inquiries, and a 1988 case in which the victims of an assault at a police lodge event were charged instead of their attackers. London's Metropolitan Police made membership something officers must declare in 2025, and 397 officers and staff have since declared it.

Italy shows how far a secret lodge can go: P2, a lodge run by businessman Licio Gelli, had on its 1981 membership list the heads of all three intelligence services, the chief of defence staff and nearly two hundred military officers, and Gelli and a P2 intelligence general were convicted of planting false evidence to mislead the inquiry into the 1980 Bologna station bombing. Italy then banned secret associations that try to influence public bodies, and still prosecutes under that law, including against a senior judge.

Declaration rules let people ask whether the officer arresting them or the judge hearing their case belongs to the same lodge as the other party. Where there is no such rule, as in most countries, people have no way of finding out.
uncertain: Gelli and others were acquitted of conspiring against the state through P2. The Romanian and Gabonese cases rest on press reports of membership, not official findings.

title: French lodges and African presidencies
roles: Head of state or minister in a lodge
case_role: Head of state or minister in a lodge

countries.note: The Grande Loge Nationale Française and the Grand Orient de France sponsored or chartered lodges in former colonies; the GLNF's grand master installed Ali Bongo as grand master of Gabon's lodge in 2009. Jacques Foccart's Service d'Action Civique ran France's African networks from the Élysée.

summary:
Across the former French colonies of West and Central Africa, presidents and senior ministers have often belonged to Masonic lodges, many of them tied to lodges in France. Freemasonry is a lawful society whose members meet privately in lodges and swear oaths of mutual support; a grand lodge is the national body over them. In several of these countries the head of state has also been the head of the national grand lodge, so the same man leads the government and the private society that his ministers, police chiefs and senior officials belong to.

The habit of using lodges to steer appointments has roots in France itself, where in 1904 lodges of the Grand Orient, France's largest Masonic body, were found to have kept files on army officers that the war ministry used to decide promotions.

Gabon is the clearest example in Africa. Omar Bongo, president from 1967 to 2009, founded and led the country's lodges, and the head of a French grand lodge installed his son Ali as grand master in the same year Ali became president. The arrangement outlasted the 2023 coup that removed Ali Bongo: the lodges kept a state official as grand master, and the head of the Grand Orient reportedly met the coup leader in secret and offered support. Press reporting in France and Africa has named the presidents or senior ministers of Congo, the Central African Republic, Chad, Niger, Burkina Faso, Mali, Guinea, Côte d'Ivoire and Senegal as lodge members or lodge leaders. In Cameroon, Le Monde reported in 1999 that President Paul Biya paid tens of millions of francs to a French Templar order, part of it from the state oil company.

The arrangement is older than independence. In Liberia, lodge membership was treated as a requirement for leading the ruling party until the 1980 coup.

For citizens of these countries, it means a president and his ministers can settle matters in meetings that parliament and the press cannot attend, sometimes with French lodge leaders present. People cannot tell whether an appointment, a contract or French backing came through official channels or through lodge contacts. Ordinary lodge members are not accused of anything, and most of this record comes from press reports, not court cases.
uncertain: Most memberships rest on press reports, mainly Jeune Afrique in 2012, and several presidents have not confirmed them. No court has found that a lodge directed a government decision in these countries. Senegal's president Macky Sall denied the membership his opponents claimed. The Grand Orient leader's meeting with Gabon's coup leader is known from press reports.

title: Rhodes, Milner and the Round Table network

countries.note: Rhodes's trustees, Milner, the Round Table journal (from 1910), Chatham House (1920) and the Pilgrims Society's London branch. Members held the posts of War Cabinet minister (Milner, 1916–18), the prime minister's private secretary (Philip Kerr, 1916–21) and editor of The Times (Geoffrey Dawson, 1912–19 and 1923–41).

Milner was High Commissioner from 1897. After 1902 his young staff ran the Transvaal and Orange River Colony administrations and worked for the 1910 Union. Patrick Duncan, one of them, became Governor-General in 1937.
Round Table group from 1909; Earl Grey, a Rhodes trustee, was Governor General 1904–11.
Round Table group from 1910; Quigley names Australia and Canada as the first dominion institutes of international affairs (1927).

summary:
This pattern explains where today's leading foreign-policy institutes, Chatham House in London and the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR) in New York, came from. Both grew out of a network of British imperialists formed around Cecil Rhodes, the mining magnate and premier of the Cape Colony, and Alfred Milner, Britain's High Commissioner in South Africa. The offices its members held are on the public record; the claim that they formed one secret society rests mainly on the historian Carroll Quigley.

The network worked by placing a small circle of like-minded men, most of them from Oxford, merchant banks and later Wall Street law firms, in the posts where imperial and foreign policy was made, and by giving them private clubs and journals in which to agree on that policy first. It began in South Africa, where from 1901 Milner filled the government of the conquered Boer republics with young Oxford graduates, known as Milner's Kindergarten, who went on to press for the union of the colonies in 1910. Over the next forty years men from the same circle sat in Britain's War Cabinet, ran the prime minister's private office, edited The Times, served as Governors General of Canada and South Africa and represented Britain in Washington.

In 1919 a Kindergarten member, Lionel Curtis, convened the Paris meeting that led to Chatham House. Its American counterpart, the CFR, ran confidential postwar planning for the US State Department during the Second World War, paid for by the Rockefeller Foundation. A 1977 study found that more than half of the senior US officials it surveyed for 1945 to 1972 were CFR members, and men moved back and forth between its leadership and the top of the CIA, the War Department and the World Bank.

For the public, the result was that a few hundred men had regular private access to ministers and wrote papers that governments then used. Membership of these bodies was and is lawful, and much of what they did was in public view; what voters could not see was how much of policy had been drafted in their private meetings before it reached government.
uncertain: The claim that these men formed one secret society rests mainly on Carroll Quigley's books. The documented part is a set of lawful clubs and public appointments.

title: The anticommunist web, 1945–1990

countries.note: Gladio, disclosed by Prime Minister Andreotti on 24 October 1990, and P2, whose 1981 list held the heads of all three intelligence services. Italy is where the stay-behind and lodge networks overlapped most.
The Chilean intelligence service DINA under Manuel Contreras called the founding meeting of Operation Condor in Santiago in November 1975.
CIA support for the stay-behind networks is confirmed in the Italian and Belgian inquiries; Condor's 1976 bombing of Orlando Letelier in Washington was carried out by DINA agents.

summary:
Some of today's arrangements go back to the Cold War. Between 1945 and 1990, governments in western Europe, Scandinavia, Turkey, Greece and Latin America, fearing communism, built secret structures inside their own states: armed networks hidden in intelligence services, officers' societies, a secret Masonic lodge and an international anticommunist league. Many of them answered to people outside the elected government, and some were paid for from abroad.

NATO countries set up 'stay-behind' networks: groups of armed civilians with hidden weapons caches, meant to resist a Soviet invasion and run by military intelligence with NATO coordination and, in some countries, NATO, British or US money. Most parliaments did not know they existed until Italy's prime minister disclosed Italy's network, called Gladio, which had 622 members, in 1990; others in Belgium, Switzerland and Turkey were then exposed or disbanded. Switzerland's official report on its network is sealed until 2041. In Sweden a secret intelligence bureau reported to the governing party rather than to parliament. Alongside these networks, officers' societies and ultranationalist groups worked with police and ministers: in Greece members of a secret officers' society led the 1967 coup, and in Turkey the leader of the Grey Wolves, an ultranationalist movement whose gunmen later worked with police, served as deputy prime minister. In Latin America, leaders of the World Anti-Communist League reached Guatemala's vice-presidency and Argentina's military command.

The clearest single case is P2, a secret Masonic lodge in Italy run by Licio Gelli. Its 1981 membership list held 962 names, among them members of parliament, serving ministers, nearly two hundred military officers and the heads of all three intelligence services, and in Argentina it included junta officers, ministers, ambassadors and an interim president. Publishing the list brought down Italy's government. Foreign intelligence services also bought influence in friendly countries, as South Korea's did with members of the US Congress in the 1970s.

For people living under these arrangements, the police, army and intelligence services answered partly to networks no voter had heard of, and governments could not be held to account for what those networks did. Families of people killed in that period are still waiting on courts: in 2025 Italian judges made final a verdict that named Gelli as the knowing financier of the 1980 Bologna station bombing. Italy's 1982 ban on secret associations came out of the P2 affair and is still in use.
uncertain: Rome courts acquitted Gelli and others of conspiring against the state through P2. The role of the secret officers' society in Greece's 1967 coup rests on historical accounts, not a court finding, and several Argentine names come from lodge lists rather than proof of active membership.

summary:
Many of the ways money is hidden inside the banking system today were worked out by two banks of the 1970s and 1980s that served governments, intelligence figures and criminals: Italy's Banco Ambrosiano and BCCI, the Bank of Credit and Commerce International. Their records, spread across 14 countries from the Americas to the Gulf and the Vatican, show the methods plainly, and the same methods are still in use.

The first method is the front owner. A bank, or the state behind it, buys other banks through people who appear to own them on their own account, so regulators never see who is in control. BCCI, mostly owned by the Abu Dhabi government and ruling family by 1991, secretly controlled First American, the largest bank in Washington, through fronts that included a former Saudi intelligence chief, while US regulators were told it was not involved; it did the same in California and Brazil.

The second is buying the officials who supervise or deposit with the bank. The practice is older than BCCI: J.P. Morgan kept a 'preferred list', exposed in 1933, of politicians and officials, Calvin Coolidge among them, who could buy shares below market price. BCCI paid off politicians' debts in the United States and Panama, made payments to people close to presidents, and was accused of paying central bank officials in Argentina and Peru to win deposits of government reserves.

The third is routing money through offshore companies and through institutions that national courts cannot reach. Banco Ambrosiano collapsed in 1982 with about $1.3 billion missing through offshore firms tied to the Vatican Bank, its main shareholder; Italy's top court ruled that a treaty kept the Vatican Bank's president out of reach of Italian courts. Ambrosiano's chairman belonged to P2, a secret Masonic lodge whose membership list of 962 names included ministers, generals and the heads of Italy's intelligence services.

For depositors and taxpayers, the losses arrived when the banks failed, and officials who banked or borrowed there had escaped checks at home. Front owners, offshore companies, banks in small jurisdictions and treaties that place some institutions outside national courts are still how hidden money moves. Most of this came out only after the banks collapsed.
uncertain: Robert Altman, First American's president, was acquitted, and the state case against its chairman Clark Clifford was dropped because of his health. The Argentine and Peruvian officials named in the BCCI bribery allegations denied them. P2's leader was convicted of fraud over Ambrosiano's collapse but acquitted in 1996 of conspiracy against the state.

title: Sworn brotherhoods that chose who governed

countries.note: Every prime minister and state president from D. F. Malan (1948) to F. W. de Klerk (1989–94) was a member of the Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret Afrikaner men's society founded in 1918. Its membership list was published by journalists Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom in 1978.

Army officers who later founded the Black Hand killed King Alexander Obrenović in 1903 and its leader, Colonel Dragutin Dimitrijević 'Apis', became head of military intelligence; its rival, the White Hand, put General Petar Živković in power as prime minister in 1929.
IDEA, a secret society of army officers, prepared the April 1967 coup; the colonels ruled until 1974 and were tried in 1975.

The Society of St. Tammany ran New York City's Democratic machine; the Know Nothings won Massachusetts in 1854; the 1920s Klan elected governors in Indiana, Colorado and Oregon and helped send Hugo Black to the Senate and then the Supreme Court.

summary:
In a number of countries during the 19th and 20th centuries, a sworn society with secret or semi-secret membership decided who governed. The societies were of three kinds: ethnic or religious fraternities that filled cabinets and city halls with their members, white-supremacist and anti-immigrant orders that won elections in parts of the United States, and secret officers' societies inside armies that took power by force. Most of these arrangements ended by the 1990s, but the laws, institutions and divisions they built are still felt.

South Africa is the fullest case. Every prime minister and state president from 1948 to 1994 belonged to the Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret Afrikaner men's society founded in 1918, and by 1979 so did all but two cabinet ministers and the heads of the army and the intelligence service. Its members wrote and ran apartheid, and the list stayed hidden until journalists printed it in 1978.

The Orange Order, a Protestant fraternity, held office in the same way in Northern Ireland and Canada. Every prime minister of Northern Ireland from 1921 to 1969 belonged to it. For the first half of the 20th century Toronto's city hall was run by its members: every mayor in that period belonged to it, as did four Canadian prime ministers. A rival French-Canadian secret society worked to place its members in federal posts, and in Ireland members of a Catholic order sat in the 1948 cabinet.

In the United States in the 1920s the Ku Klux Klan, a white-supremacist secret society, backed or supplied governors in at least four states and put members in city police forces; one Klan member reached the Supreme Court before his membership was known. In Serbia and Greece, secret officers' societies inside the army supplied prime ministers and led coups.

For people outside the society, this meant laws made and enforced by one closed group. Black South Africans lived under apartheid laws written by a cabinet drawn almost entirely from one secret body, and Catholic families in parts of the United States faced laws aimed at their schools. Where members filled a police force or civil service, appointments and arrests favoured them; as recently as 2014 two Florida officers were removed over Klan ties and their past arrests reviewed for racial profiling.
uncertain: Several membership claims rest on single reports or later books, such as the accounts of the Catholic order's members in Ireland's 1948 cabinet.

summary:
This pattern explains where today's government-funded democracy grants, such as those of the US National Endowment for Democracy (NED), came from. From the late 1940s to 1967, the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) secretly paid for student, labour, cultural and broadcasting groups at home and abroad, all of which presented themselves as private.

The method was to pass government money through organisations that looked independent: private foundations, trade-union committees, student federations, cultural bodies and broadcasters. That let the CIA fund anti-communist writers, unions, radio stations and election campaigns in Western Europe, Latin America and Asia without the readers, members or voters knowing who was paying. The Senate's Church Committee found CIA money in nearly half of the international grants made by a group of 164 US foundations in the mid-1960s. Its largest cultural operation, the Congress for Cultural Freedom, was run from Paris by a CIA officer, had offices in 35 countries and published more than 20 magazines. Radio Free Europe and Radio Liberty, which broadcast into the Soviet bloc from Germany, ran on CIA money, as did the Asia Foundation and the main US national student association. Some of the money went straight into elections, as in Brazil in 1962, when a CIA-linked institute paid for opposition candidates for Congress and state governorships.

Press reports in 1966 and 1967 exposed the funding, and most of it was then cut or moved into open government budgets. Congress created NED in 1983 and funds it through yearly appropriations, and one of its founders said in 1991 that much of its work had been done covertly by the CIA 25 years earlier.

For the people who read these magazines, joined these unions or listened to these stations, it meant taking part in groups shaped by a foreign intelligence service they did not know was paying. In Italy, Brazil and elsewhere, US money went to one side before national elections. Today the Russian and Chinese governments point to this history when they ban or sanction foreign-funded groups; NED was the first organisation Russia declared 'undesirable', in 2015.

summary:
From the 1950s to the 1980s, US government aid and the Ford Foundation, an American private foundation, paid for economists from poorer countries to take degrees at American universities. Some of those graduates later ran their own countries' economies under military governments, bringing the thinking of the schools that trained them into the ministries that set budgets, taxes, borrowing and interest rates. The record on this map covers Chile and Indonesia.

The method was slow and indirect. Money paid for a link between a US university and a local one, students went abroad for years, and when a general seized power and wanted a ready-made economic team, the graduates were there with a plan. In Chile, economists trained at the University of Chicago, known as the 'Chicago Boys', wrote the economic programme that General Pinochet's government adopted in 1975 and then held the economy and finance ministries and the central bank until the 1982 debt crisis. In Indonesia, economists trained at the University of California, Berkeley, later called the 'Berkeley Mafia', became General Suharto's economic team after 1966 and ran planning and finance for well over a decade.

This is not bribery or spying. The outside money paid for training years before anyone took office, and the governments that appointed these men chose them freely. What it produced was a small group, trained on foreign money and sharing one school's ideas, that wrote national economic policy for more than a decade in each country.

For people in Chile and Indonesia, it meant living under economic plans drawn up by officials they had not elected, appointed by generals who had taken power by force. When those plans worked, as Indonesia's did against runaway inflation in the late 1960s, the public had no voice in them, and when they failed, as Chile's did in the 1982 debt crisis, people bore the cost without having been asked.

title: Exposure, purge and reversal

timeline.event: US Senate Church Committee begins hearings on intelligence abuses

summary:
Across the cases on this map, from more than 80 countries and stretching from the 1890s to today, infiltration usually comes to light in one of a few ways: a seized membership list, a leak to journalists, a parliamentary or judicial inquiry, a UN investigation, another government's sanctions, or occasionally an accident that puts a wanted man and an official in the same place. Very little of it is found by the institution that was infiltrated. What follows is often a purge, and then, in a large share of cases, a partial or full reversal.

Exposure can be sudden and large. When Italian police found the membership list of P2, a secret Masonic lodge, in 1981, it named ministers, generals and the heads of all three intelligence services, and parliament dissolved the lodge and banned secret associations. Purges can be just as large, and are often carried out by decree. Governments remove judges, police officers and civil servants in their thousands, often without an individual hearing for each. Italy's government has dissolved town councils and health authorities found to be under mafia influence 402 times since 1991, many of them more than once.

Reversals follow in many countries. Courts annul convictions because evidence was gathered illegally or the wrong court heard the case, as Brazil's Supreme Court did with Lula's corruption convictions in 2021. Prosecutions lapse because time limits have run out. Purged officials win their jobs back in court, and people named by inquiries or under foreign sanctions return to office, sometimes at the top of government. Bans on secret societies inside the state can lapse when the government changes: in South Africa an order for civil servants to leave the secret Afrikaner Broederbond lapsed in 1948, and every prime minister and state president from then until 1994 was a member.

For people in these countries, a sanction or commission report tells them what a government or inquiry concluded, not what a court proved. A purge by decree can remove people with no proven link, and a case thrown out on procedure leaves the original accusation neither confirmed nor cleared.
uncertain: Many cases rest on one government's sanctions or one inquiry's findings, which no court has heard.
